issues.message: The second occurrence of ٱلَّذِى reuses the first occurrence's teachingId even though its authored sentence role and learner takeaway are occurrence-specific. This can collapse the 107:2 context during lesson assembly or runtime lookup.
issues.requiredAction: Assign 107:2:2 an occurrence-specific teaching ID, or use an explicit shared lexical lesson plus an occurrence override so the identifying role after ذَٰلِكَ remains attached to this occurrence.

evidence.comparison: 107:1:2 introduces the person being considered; 107:2:2 identifies ذَٰلِكَ through يَدُعُّ ٱلْيَتِيمَ.

issues.message: The learner-facing construction writes رَأَيْتَ, while the canonical occurrence is أَرَءَيْتَ and the segmented stem is رَءَيْتَ. Without a normalization note, the learner sees an unexplained spelling change inside the same lesson.
issues.requiredAction: Use the canonical رَءَيْتَ in the Arabic construction, or explicitly label رَأَيْتَ as a normalized citation spelling and show how it corresponds to the preserved Qur'anic form.

issues.message: Root letters are formatted inconsistently across the seven-ayah batch: this field uses spaces (ر أ ي), while other authored fields use hyphens (ر-أ-ي, ص-ل-و, م ن ع). The same root therefore appears in two learner-facing conventions.
issues.requiredAction: Choose one root-letter separator and apply it consistently to every authored root, root picture, form entry, and learner connection in ayat 1–7.

issues.message: The phrase sun-letter-free noun is not a clear learner recognition term and incorrectly puts the focus on the noun rather than on the article's pronunciation before ي.
issues.requiredAction: Replace it with a standard, concrete cue such as: ٱلْ is pronounced clearly here because ي is a moon letter; or omit the sun/moon-letter aside if it is not needed for this lesson.

evidence.draftText: Recognize ٱلْ as the definite article before a sun-letter-free noun.
evidence.learnerRisk: The learner may not know whether the noun or article is being classified, or why the lām remains audible.
